title: Evolution
subject: Science
purpose: Explain how evidence supports evolution and how heritable variation, selection pressures and reproduction can change populations over generations.
prior: Elicit prior ideas about traits, inheritance, fossils, adaptations and environmental change. Check students can distinguish an individual from a population.
future: Use these ideas as a foundation for deeper study of inheritance, biodiversity and evidence for relationships between organisms. Confirm later sequencing with the department.
knowledgeSummary: 12 selected Ministry knowledge statements, organised into 4 learning focuses: Evidence and common ancestry; Variation and selection pressures; Natural selection over generations; New species and extinction.
practicesSummary:
Evaluate by: Analysing evidence from evolutionary contexts (e.g. fossil records, trait variations, or environmental changes) to show how theories develop over time.
Communicate by: Interpreting a set of fossil images to infer an organism's structure and likely environment.
Apply by: Examining the role of environmental change on extinction of species (e.g. habitat destruction, change in temperature).

Teacher preparation: select age-appropriate examples and models for each focus; prepare a diagnostic task and an unfamiliar transfer task. Check practical requirements before teaching.
assessment: Students explain a change in trait frequency in an unfamiliar population across several generations. They connect heritable variation, a named selection pressure, differential reproduction and population change, and use evidence to support the explanation. Include a fossil inference or extinction example relevant to the selected focuses.
descriptors: Look for accurate concepts and vocabulary, a coherent explanation, and a justified link between evidence and claims. Agree task-specific descriptors and reporting judgements using the school’s Junior Assessment Framework before assessment.
reporting: Record demonstrated learning, supporting evidence and one next step. Moderate judgements with the department using the agreed school framework.

focuses.title: Evidence and common ancestry
focuses.knowledge:
Fossils provide evidence that organisms have appeared in many different forms throughout Earth's history, with some similar to organisms alive today (e.g. crocodiles), while others belong to extinct groups that no longer exist (e.g. trilobites).
Evidence (e.g. fossils, shared traits, DNA evidence) supports the theory that populations and species have changed over time.
Evidence collected to date supports the theory that all living organisms are related through common ancestry (e.g. shared features among vertebrates).
focuses.practices:
Analysing evidence from evolutionary contexts (e.g. fossil records, trait variations, or environmental changes) to show how theories develop over time.
Interpreting a set of fossil images to infer an organism's structure and likely environment.
focuses.objectives: Use fossil features, shared traits and DNA evidence to support an explanation of common ancestry.
focuses.vocabulary:
Tier 2: Evidence; infer; justify.
Tier 3: Fossil; extinct; common ancestor; DNA.
focuses.misconceptions: A fossil is always a bone; organisms alive today are unchanged ancestors of other living species.
focuses.checks: Give students unfamiliar fossil images. Ask them to infer structure and environment, then distinguish an observation from an inference.

focuses.title: Variation and selection pressures
focuses.knowledge:
Individuals within a species show variation in their traits (e.g. differences in male wētā head and jaw size).
Some variation is heritable, meaning it can be passed from parents to offspring.
Features of the environment that affect survival or reproduction are called selection pressures (e.g. limited food).
focuses.practices: Analysing evidence from evolutionary contexts (e.g. fossil records, trait variations, or environmental changes) to show how theories develop over time.
focuses.objectives: Distinguish variation from heritable variation and identify a selection pressure in a named population.
focuses.vocabulary:
Tier 2: Variation; distinguish; influence.
Tier 3: Trait; heritable; selection pressure; population.
focuses.misconceptions: All variation can be inherited; an organism develops a useful inherited trait because it needs it.
focuses.checks: Compare inherited and acquired examples. Ask which could affect the next generation and why.

focuses.title: Natural selection over generations
focuses.knowledge:
Natural selection is a process in which heritable differences between individuals influence their chances of surviving and reproducing in the presence of selection pressures (e.g. cold extremes, sun exposure).
Contemporaries Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace presented their theories on natural selection together.
Over many generations, individuals with traits that increase survival or reproduction are more likely to leave offspring, causing those inherited traits to become more common in a population (e.g. moth camouflage increasing in frequency).
Evolution describes these changes in traits within populations over generations, not within individuals.
focuses.practices: Analysing evidence from evolutionary contexts (e.g. fossil records, trait variations, or environmental changes) to show how theories develop over time.
focuses.objectives: Explain how a selection pressure changes the frequency of a heritable trait over generations; locate Darwin and Wallace in the development of the explanation.
focuses.vocabulary:
Tier 2: Frequency; sequence; explain.
Tier 3: Natural selection; reproduction; generation; evolution.
focuses.misconceptions: Individuals evolve during their lifetime; natural selection gives every organism the traits it needs.
focuses.checks: Use a simple population model over three generations. Ask students to explain who reproduces and how the population changes, without using “needed to”.

focuses.title: New species and extinction
focuses.knowledge:
Over long periods, trait changes accumulate, resulting in new species forming from a shared ancestor (e.g. kākā, kea, and kākāpō becoming different kinds of parrots).
Some species are unable to survive environmental change and become extinct (e.g. moa).
focuses.practices: Examining the role of environmental change on extinction of species (e.g. habitat destruction, change in temperature).
focuses.objectives: Use shared ancestry and environmental change to explain how lineages may diverge or become extinct.
focuses.vocabulary:
Tier 2: Accumulate; contrast; consequence.
Tier 3: Species; speciation; extinction; ancestor.
focuses.misconceptions: Every species can adapt quickly enough to survive any environmental change.
focuses.checks: Compare a branching ancestry diagram with an extinction case. Ask students to justify what each can and cannot show.
